idiom_name: abstract Component + CustomerCore + spec-keyed role map (Class<?> keys) + cast
implementation_notes: The canonical Java realization is the paper's: an abstract Customer declares the role protocol and the shared operations, CustomerCore keeps a Map keyed by role specification (Class<?> or an enum) and creates roles through a creator lookup, and each CustomerRole subclass wraps its core and forwards every shared operation while adding its own (iluwatar's role-object module is exactly this structure, with an enum Role and an Optional-returning getRole). The alternative realization generates transparent views with java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance, which creates a class implementing exactly the requested interfaces and dispatching every call to an InvocationHandler; choose the proxy when clients want one object carrying several role interfaces, and the class hierarchy when roles have rich state and ordinary debuggable classes matter more.
pitfalls: The role map keyed by Class<?> allows one role instance per concrete role class; parametrized roles need an explicit specification object.
Role classes duplicate the forwarding of every shared operation; keep the shared interface small or generate the forwarding.
Roles hold their core and the core holds its roles - the cycle is GC-collected, but it delays finalization and surprises anyone expecting deterministic cleanup.

variants.name: Runtime proxy views over the role registry (java.lang.reflect.Proxy)
variants.idiom_name: Proxy.newProxyInstance over the core's role registry
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of forwarding subclasses, the core hands out a JDK proxy built with Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] { Borrower.class }, handler); the handler looks the requested role up in the core's specification-keyed registry and invokes the method on the role object. The proxy instance satisfies instanceof for every requested role interface and can present a combination of role interfaces per call, so clients get truly transparent views without a role class per interface. The price is reflection, interface-only dispatch (no class roles) and an extra indirection that hides the concrete role from stack traces, which is why the class hierarchy remains the default.
pitfalls: Proxy classes are final and interface-only; role objects behind the proxy lose their concrete type, so equals/hashCode and debugging need explicit handling.
Reflective invocation wraps role exceptions in InvocationTargetException, and Object methods (equals, hashCode, toString) are dispatched to the handler as the JDK documents.
